questions.question_text: Confabulation is most commonly observed in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Confabulation—the falsification of memory occurring in clear consciousness with organic pathology, manifesting as filling gaps in memory with imagined or untrue experiences—is classically associated with Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, though it also occurs in Alzheimer's disease and traumatic brain injury.

questions.question_text: A 19yearold male patient exhibits intermittent episodes of muscle weakness, especially during rest periods after strenuous exercise or a high carbohydrate meal. He tells you that his father also has been diagnosed with similar symptoms and has been presenting with a diagnosis of hypokalemic periodic paralysis. Which of the following medications can be used to prevent these attacks?
questions.explanation: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis is a rare autosomal dominant condition characterized by episodes of muscle Y BOARD REvIEw weakness that coincide with the lowering of blood potassium levels. Between episodes, muscle strength is normal. Weakness is rare during exercise, but it is triggered by resting after exercise. This condition is caused by a hereditary defect in muscle ion channels. Attacks are usually aborted with potassium chloride treatment orally. Preventive strategy includes treatment with potassiumsparing diuretic.

questions.question_text: The clinical presentation of Wernicke encephalopathy (WE) may be overlooked due to low index of ROPSYChIAtRIC DISORDERS • 109 suspicion. Which of the following conditions is linked to WE?

options.text: A diagnosis of alcohol use disorder

questions.explanation: Wernicke encephalopathy, caused by vitamin B1 deficiency, is not diagnosed in about 80% of cases. This may in part be because clinicians are looking for the full triad, which rarely occurs in the same patient. Alcohol use disorder is the most common cause of WE, but this can be present in other conditions associated with vitamin B1 deficiency such as hyperemesis gravidarum, prolonged total parenteral nutrition, and infection with HIV.

questions.question_text: Which histopathological change in Alzheimer's disease consists of hyperphosphorylated tau protein?
questions.explanation: Neurofibrillary tangles (NFT) in Alzheimer's disease are composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein, which is a cytoskeletal element and appears basophilic on staining.

questions.question_text: Frontotemporal dementia is associated with intracellular accumulations of which proteins?
questions.explanation: Frontotemporal dementia is associated with intracellular accumulations of tau and ubiquitin. Pick's disease specifically shows both tau-positive and ubiquitin-positive inclusions.

questions.question_text: What is the pathophysiological mechanism of multisystem atrophy?
questions.explanation: Multisystem atrophy is characterized by alpha-synucleinopathy with distinctive inclusion bodies in glial cells, classifying it as a synucleinopathy distinct from Parkinson's disease.

questions.question_text: Kaiser-Fleischer rings are found in which condition affecting which part of the eye?
questions.explanation: Kaiser-Fleischer rings are found in the cornea in Wilson disease when central nervous system involvement occurs. They can be identified with a slit-lamp examination, though they are not universally present. More reliable diagnosis depends on low ceruloplasmin and elevated copper in urine and liver biopsies.

questions.question_text: Which variant of frontotemporal dementia is characterized by personality changes with relatively preserved neurocognitive functioning in early stages?
questions.explanation: FTD behavioral variant is characterized by personality changes, with neurocognitive functioning often preserved in early stages.

questions.question_text: A 10yearold female child with a history of rheumatic fever comes to her pediatrician with newonset rapid, irregular movements of her limbs, trunk, and face. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sydenham chorea is seen most frequently in girls who have a history of Group A betahemolytic streptococcal infection/ rheumatic fever and is characterized by irregular movements of the limbs, trunk, and face. Movements occur as a result of autoantibodies attacking the basal ganglia. Most children recover. Pediatric acuteonset neuropsychiatric syndrome (PANS; until recently known as pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorder associated with streptococcal infection, or PANDAS) is also a disorder associated with Group A betahemolytic streptococcal infection; however, PANS is associated with onset of vocal and/ or motor tics. Tics in Tourette syndrome can usually be suppressed with effort and are stereotyped rather than irregular.

questions.question_text: The lifetime prevalence of psychosis in individuals suffering from epilepsy is around
questions.explanation: Psychosis is the specifi c psychiatric disorder most clearly associated with epilepsy. The lifelong prevalence of all psychotic disorders among epileptic patients ranges from 7% to 12%. Patients whose epilepsy has a mediobasal temporal focus are especially at risk. Studies on the laterality of the seizure focus suggest an association of a left-sided focus with psychosis. Although conclusions derived from surface EEG recording are open to criticism, depth recordings of presurgical patients show that twice as many patients with left temporal lesions have psychosis. Kaplan HI. Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 8th edn. Lippincott Williams and Wilkins, 2004, p. 379.

questions.question_text: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is classified as which motor variant of FTD?

options.text: FTD motoric variant with PSP presentation

correct_answer.text: FTD motoric variant with PSP presentation

questions.explanation: Progressive supranuclear palsy (characterized by poor balance, frequent falls, and horizontal gaze palsy) is one of three motor subtypes within the FTD motoric variant.

questions.question_text: His wife reports he has been “acting out his dreams.” When prescribed a lowdose antipsychotic, the individual became heavily sedated with muscle rigidity. The most likely diagnosis is:

options.text: Major neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies
Major neurocognitive disorder due to Parkinson disease
A diagnosis of mild neurocognitive disorder
Major neurocognitive disorder due to progressive supranuclear palsy
A diagnosis of major frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of major frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder

questions.explanation: RLS is a sensorimotor disorder in which the patient complains of a peculiar creepy or crawling feeling in the extremities. The undesirable sensation is worse or only occurs in the evening or at night, is exacerbated by keeping the limbs still, and is relieved or partially relieved by movement. The symptoms interfere with initiation and maintenance of sleep. The diagnosis of RLS is clinical, based solely on reported symptoms or symptoms observed in the patient.

questions.question_text: Which variant of frontotemporal dementia is characterized by progressive impairment in motor functioning?
questions.explanation: The motoric variant of FTD is characterized by progressive impairment in motor functioning, with three subtypes including progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal degeneration, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

questions.question_text: Which is the most commonly site for the main tumour in a metastatic brain cancer?
questions.explanation: Of patients with intracerebral metastases, 40% originate in the lung, 20% are from breast tumours, 10% are melanomas, 7% arise from the genitourinary tract, 7% from the GIT, and 5% are of gynaecological origin. Cummings JL and Mega MS. Neuropsychiatry and Behavioural Neuroscience, 2nd edn. Oxford University Press 2003, p. 402.

questions.question_text: Neurofibrillary tangles (NFT) in Alzheimer's disease are composed of which protein?
questions.explanation: NFT (neurofibrillary tangles) are composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein, which are intracellular, basophilic cytoskeletal elements.

questions.question_text: An 18yearold female patient has a 24hour history of headache, fever, and vomiting. Her roommate brings her to the emergency room after she has a seizure. T2weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveals hyperintensity of the temporal and inferior frontal lobes with a masslike effect. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hyperintensity of the temporal and inferior frontal lobes is seen in herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis.

questions.question_text: Lecanemab (Leqembi), FDA-approved in 2023 for early Alzheimer's disease, differs from earlier anti-amyloid antibodies (aducanumab) in which important way?

options.text: Lecanemab targets tau tangles rather than amyloid-beta
Lecanemab preferentially targets soluble amyloid-beta protofibrils rather than plaques
Lecanemab is a small molecule rather than a monoclonal antibody
Lecanemab requires no biomarker confirmation before treatment
Lecanemab is approved for all stages of Alzheimer's disease

correct_answer.text: Lecanemab preferentially targets soluble amyloid-beta protofibrils rather than plaques

questions.explanation: Lecanemab (BAN2401) preferentially targets soluble amyloid-beta protofibrils — the most neurotoxic form of amyloid — rather than insoluble amyloid plaques. Earlier antibodies (aducanumab, bapineuzumab) primarily targeted fibrillar plaques. Protofibrils are 3,000x more neurotoxic than monomers, making them a more therapeutically relevant target. The CLARITY AD Phase 3 trial (N=1,795) showed 27% slowing of clinical decline (CDR-SB primary endpoint) over 18 months, with significant biomarker effects (amyloid PET clearance, p-tau217 reduction, NfL stabilisation). Key adverse effect: ARIA (amyloid-related imaging abnormalities) — brain oedema/microhaemorrhages, requiring MRI monitoring. Approved for early AD (MCI or mild dementia) with confirmed amyloid pathology. NICE initially declined to recommend it in England due to modest clinical benefit relative to monitoring burden and cost. Donanemab (anti-Aβ plaques, insoluble form) received FDA approval in 2024 with slightly greater efficacy in tau-low patients.

questions.question_text: Depression, irritability, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, and apathy are frequently linked to Huntington’s disease and often precede the onset of motor symptoms. Psychosis more rarely precedes the onset of motor symptoms. which of the following options is a core feature of major or mild neurocognitive disorder due to Huntington’s disease?

options.text: Progressive cognitive impairment with early changes in executive function.
Prominent early memory impairment, mostly affecting short-term memory.
Psychosis in the early stages, with marked olfactory hallucinations.
A diagnosis of chorea (involuntary jerking movements).
A diagnosis of anosmia (loss of smell).

correct_answer.text: Progressive cognitive impairment with early changes in executive function.

questions.explanation: A core feature of Huntington’s disease is progressive cognitive impairment with early changes in executive function (i.e., processing speed, organization, and planning) rather than learning and memory. Cognitive and associated behavioral changes often precede the emergence of the typical motor abnormalities of bradykinesia (i.e., slowing of voluntary movement) and chorea (i.e., involuntary jerking movements).

questions.question_text: GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide) are being actively investigated for neuroprotective effects in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease. Which mechanism is most directly proposed?

options.text: Peripheral weight loss reducing systemic inflammation only
Central GLP-1R activation promoting neuronal survival, reducing alpha-synuclein aggregation and neuroinflammation
Insulin sensitisation in peripheral tissues without CNS effects
Dopamine receptor agonism in the substantia nigra
Tau phosphorylation inhibition via insulin signalling cascade

correct_answer.text: Central GLP-1R activation promoting neuronal survival, reducing alpha-synuclein aggregation and neuroinflammation

questions.explanation: GLP-1 receptors (GLP-1R) are expressed in substantia nigra, hippocampus, cortex, and hypothalamus. Central GLP-1R activation promotes: (1) Neuronal survival via PI3K/Akt/mTOR and MAPK signalling; (2) Reduced alpha-synuclein aggregation and toxicity (shown in rodent and C. elegans PD models); (3) Reduced neuroinflammation (microglial activation, IL-6, TNF-a suppression); (4) Improved insulin signalling in neurons (relevant to Alzheimer's disease as a 'type 3 diabetes'); (5) Mitochondrial protection and autophagy enhancement. The EXENATIDE-PD Phase 2 trial (Athauda et al., Lancet 2017) showed that exenatide (weekly SC injection) significantly maintained motor function in Parkinson's patients vs placebo over 48 weeks. Multiple Phase 3 trials are ongoing (semaglutide for PD and AD). Semaglutide's large Phase 3 cardiovascular trials (SUSTAIN-6, PIONEER-6) also showed reduced stroke and cognitive endpoints — supporting CNS benefits beyond weight loss.

questions.question_text: Expressed as a percentile, what is the typical performance on neuropsychological testing of patients with major neurocognitive disorder (NCD)?

options.text: A diagnosis of sixtieth percentile or below.
A diagnosis of fiftieth percentile or below.
A diagnosis of twenty-fifth percentile or below.
A diagnosis of sixteenth percentile or below.
A diagnosis of third percentile or below.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of third percentile or below.

questions.explanation: Neuropsychological testing, with performance compared with norms appropriate to the patient’s age, educational attainment, and cultural background, is part of the standard evaluation of NCDs. For major NCD, performance is typically 2 or more standard deviations below appropriate norms (3rd percentile or below). For mild NCD, performance typically lies in the 1–2 standard deviation range (between the 3rd and 16th percentiles).

questions.question_text: Which neuropathological feature of Alzheimer's disease is extracellular and eosinophilic?
questions.explanation: Senile plaques are insoluble amyloid peptide deposits that appear as eosinophilic masses (apple green) and are extracellular.

questions.question_text: A patient with Huntington's disease typically demonstrates which characteristic gait pattern?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease characteristically presents with a lurching, chaotic gait pattern, distinct from the scissoring gait of upper motor neuron lesions and the broad, unsteady gait of cerebellar disease.

questions.question_text: Which enzyme is deficient in acute intermittent porphyria?
questions.explanation: Acute intermittent porphyria is characterized by partial deficiency of hydroxymethylbilane synthase (also known as porphobilinogen deaminase). This enzyme deficiency results in accumulation of porphyrin precursors. The condition is autosomal dominant, presents with abdominal pain, neuropathies, and constipation, and can be triggered by certain medications including barbiturates, benzodiazepines, and sulpiride.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is often the primary site for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection in children?
questions.explanation: In children, the brain is often a primary site for HIV infection, leading to decreased brain development and often presenting with encephalitis, memory, concentration, and attentional issues.

questions.question_text: Which of the following protein inclusion profiles is most common in frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation: The most common protein inclusion profile in frontotemporal dementia is tau-positive, amyloid-negative, though ubiquitin-positive inclusions are also frequently observed; familial FTD is typically ubiquitin-positive and tau-negative.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a core clinical feature of Lewy body dementia?

options.text: Fluctuating cognition with notable variation in attention and alertness

questions.explanation: While Lewy body dementia presents with progressive cognitive decline, memory loss may not be an early feature, distinguishing it from Alzheimer's disease where memory loss is typically prominent early.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is not caused by the antibodies found in myasthenia gravis?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine (ACh) receptors at the neuromuscular junction are nicotinic; those in the central nervous system are muscarinic. As such, the nicotinic ACh receptor antibodies found in myasthenia gravis affect only strength, not cognition. Patients with myasthenia gravis do not have cognitive impairment related to the condition— though they certainly may have cognitive impairment of alternate etiology.

questions.question_text: What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism of Korsakoff syndrome?

options.text: Mamillary body and dorsomedial thalamic dysfunction from thiamine deficiency

correct_answer.text: Mamillary body and dorsomedial thalamic dysfunction from thiamine deficiency

questions.explanation: Korsakoff syndrome results from thiamine deficiency causing dysfunction of alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and pyruvate dehydrogenase, leading to lesions in mamillary bodies, dorsomedial thalamus, and related tracts.

questions.question_text: In children, which of the following is the most serious neurological adverse consequence of lead poisoning?
questions.explanation: The most serious neurological complication of lead poising in children is delirium and its associated potential for lasting neurocognitive deficits.

questions.question_text: In Lewy body dementia, alpha-synuclein accumulates primarily in which brain region?

options.text: Temporal lobe, cingulate gyrus, frontal lobes, and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

correct_answer.text: Temporal lobe, cingulate gyrus, frontal lobes, and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

questions.explanation: Alpha-synuclein accumulation in Lewy body dementia is found in the temporal lobe, cingulate gyrus, frontal lobes, and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is most commonly seen psychiatric manifestation of Cushing’s syndrome?
questions.explanation: Full depressive syndrome has been reported in up to 70% of people with Cushing’s syndrome. The most common cause of Cushing’s syndrome is pharmacological. Cushing’s disease is a primary pituitary tumour, which secretes an excess of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). Psychiatric manifestations may be due to the direct effects of elevated corticosteroids on the neurons or due to hypothalamic dysfunction. The neocortex and hippocampus have glucocorticoid receptors, the action on which could explain the cognitive and mood disorder seen in these patients. Cushing’s disease has been associated with a reduction in hippocampal volume, which is reversed on correction of steroid levels. There is also some evidence to show that stress could be associated with exacerbation of the illness. Levenson JL. Essentials of Psychosomatic Medicine, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Press, 2006, p. 96.

questions.question_text: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) linked to the MAPT gene mutation is pathologically characterized by the presence of:
questions.explanation: Familial FTD linked to chromosome 17q21 (the MAPT gene) is characterized by tau-positive inclusions, historically referred to as Pick bodies.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a human prion disease?
questions.explanation: Human prion diseases include Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD), variant CJD (vCJD—associated with BSE), Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker Syndrome, Fatal Familial Insomnia, and Kuru; bovine spongiform encephalopathy and scrapie are animal prion diseases.

questions.question_text: Which autoimmune encephalitis antibody is most associated with prodromal flu-like illness, psychosis, and oral dyskinesia?
questions.explanation: NMDA-receptor mediated autoimmune encephalitis presents with sudden cognitive decline after viral prodrome, psychosis, repetitive chewing (oral dyskinesia), and seizures.

questions.question_text: A 72yearold female patient with hypertension and hyperlipidemia is brought to the emergency room for evaluation of the sensation of the “room spinning.” She has difficulty sitting unsupported and leans to one side. Her symptoms began suddenly. Exam is notable for leftsided ptosis and miosis, and decreased pain and temperature sensation on her left face and right trunk and limbs. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Posterior cerebral artery transient ischemic attack

questions.explanation: Lateral medullary infarct (Wallenberg syndrome) presents with dizziness/ vertigo, facial pain, difficulty sitting without support, hoarseness, and dysphagia. Exam may be notable for Horner syndrome, limb ataxia, laryngeal paralysis, and pharyngeal paralysis. Classic for this type of stroke is ipsilateral decreased pain and temperature sensation on the face and contralateral decreased pain and temperature sensation in the trunk and limbs.

questions.question_text: Which is true regarding confabulation

options.text: There is subjective awareness of memory loss
It can only occur in Korsakoff syndrome
There is deliberate falsification of facts

questions.explanation: Confabulation involves unconscious filling of memory gaps with fabricated information, often affecting autobiographical memory. It is not deliberate falsification, can occur in various conditions beyond Korsakoff syndrome (including clouded consciousness), and patients typically lack awareness of the confabulation.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which features differentiates central vertigo from peripheral vertigo?

options.text: Central vertigo is often linked to tinnitus.
Nystagmus is always bidirectional in peripheral vertigo.
Central vertigo is most often caused by a middle cerebral artery lesion.
Visual fixation does not obliterate central vertigo.

correct_answer.text: Visual fixation does not obliterate central vertigo.

questions.explanation: Central vertigo is more commonly seen in posterior circulation stroke. Unlike peripheral vertigo, central vertigo is rarely associated with tinnitus. It starts immediately, without any time lag between head movement and onset of symptoms. It is rarely associated with horizontal nystagmus. The nystagmus does not go away with visual fixation.

questions.question_text: A 57yearold female patient with no known medical history exhibits newonset, dull, moderate, unilateral pain over the left side of her head and behind the left eye. She reports no history of headaches but has been experiencing fatigue and weight loss for several weeks. Pain has been so unbearable that she has not been able to comb her hair. The individual came urgently to see you after she experienced a brief period of transient vision loss. What is the next step in the clinical approach of this individual?
questions.explanation: The vignette describes a likely case of giant cell arteritis. The condition is rare in individuals younger than 50 years old. Temporal artery biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis of giant cell arteritis; however, treatment with glucocorticoids should not be delayed for biopsy results. This is especially the case when the patient already presents with visual loss and where intravenous methylprednisone is indicated. Other diagnostic tests including ESR, CRP, MRI, and ultrasound are useful but not required before treatment initiation.

questions.question_text: In familial frontotemporal dementia caused by mutations in the MAPT gene (FTDP-17), which neuropathological finding is characteristic?
questions.explanation:
In MAPT-linked familial FTD (FTDP-17), tau-positive neuronal and glial inclusions are the defining neuropathological feature, reflecting mutations that alter the ratio of 3R to 4R tau isoforms.

in familial FTD broadly, TDP-43 (option E) is the most representative marker, as GRN and C9orf72 mutations together are more common than MAPT mutations and both produce TDP-43 pathology. 
tau-positive inclusions such as Pick bodies also contain ubiquitin. Beta-amyloid (option A) is characteristic of Alzheimer\'s disease, and alpha-synuclein (option D) is characteristic of Lewy body disorders.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is considered the cardinal feature of delirium?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of delirium is defi ned by psychopathology and temporal course. It is usually of acute onset and the cardinal feature is a disturbance in consciousness. Impairment of consciousness is the key feature that separates delirium from most other psychiatric disorders. There is a continuum between mild impairment of consciousness and near unconsciousness. There is fl uctuation in intensity, and symptoms are often worse at night. The other features are an inability to focus and maintain attention, perceptual disturbances, disorientation in time and/or space, rarely to people (though false recognition is common) and almost never to self. Disorientation to time is often the first warning sign of delirium. Attention is poor and the patient is easily distractable, looking either apathetic or intensely focused upon something. Psychomotor disturbance may be in the form of agitation or retardation. Other features may include lability of mood and incoherent speech. Gelder M, Harrison P, and Cowen P. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006; p. 329.

questions.question_text: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is an autoimmune condition where autoantibodies target the GluN1 subunit of NMDA receptors. Which clinical triad most characteristically presents in the early stages of this condition?
questions.explanation: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (anti-NMDAR-E), the most common autoimmune encephalitis, was first described by Dalmau in 2007. The characteristic clinical progression: (1) Prodrome: flu-like symptoms; (2) Psychiatric phase: acute psychosis, mania, anxiety, personality change — often initially misdiagnosed as first-episode schizophrenia or bipolar disorder; (3) Neurological phase: seizures, movement disorders (orofacial dyskinesias, choreoathetosis, catatonia), autonomic instability (tachycardia, hyperthermia, labile BP), reduced consciousness, and in severe cases, hypoventilation requiring ventilation. It predominantly affects young women; ~50% have an associated ovarian teratoma. Diagnosis requires CSF or serum anti-GluN1 (anti-NR1) antibodies. Treatment: tumour removal (if present) + immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange; rituximab/cyclophosphamide second line). Most patients recover fully with treatment, though recovery takes months. This condition is critical for psychiatrists to recognise as it initially presents with psychiatric features and requires urgent medical investigation.

questions.question_text: Seizures originating from the parietal lobe typically begin with which type of aura?
questions.explanation: Parietal lobe seizures characteristically begin with contralateral somatosensory aura, usually of the positive type such as electrical sensation or tingling.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is a core feature of major or mild neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies?

options.text: Fluctuating cognition with pronounced variations in attention and alertness.
A diagnosis of early memory loss.
Spontaneous features of parkinsonism, with onset at least 1 year prior to development of cognitive decline.
Fulfillment of criteria for rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder.
Evidence of low striatal dopamine transporter uptake in basal ganglia as demonstrated by single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) or positron emission tomography (PET) imaging.

correct_answer.text: Fluctuating cognition with pronounced variations in attention and alertness.

questions.explanation: Recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations (not auditory hallucinations) and parkinsonism arising after (not earlier than) cognitive impair420 | Neurocognitive Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE ment are the other core features of major or mild neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies. REM sleep behavioral disorder and excessive sensitivity to neuroleptic agents are “suggestive diagnostic features”; low dopamine transporter uptake in basal ganglia is a diagnostic marker but is not included in the diagnostic criteria.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a form of frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is not a form of frontotemporal dementia; it is a neurodegenerative disorder affecting the basal ganglia. Progressive supranuclear palsy was historically thought to be related to Parkinson's disease but is now considered related to frontotemporal dementia.

questions.question_text: Which is a human prion disease?
questions.explanation: Fatal familial insomnia is a rare, invariably fatal autosomal dominant neurodegenerative prion disease caused by mutation of the PRNP gene. Other human prion diseases include Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker syndrome, and kuru.

questions.question_text: Which protein inclusion profile is most common in frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation: The most common protein inclusion profile in frontotemporal dementia is tau positive with amyloid negative. The classification is based on protein inclusion types including tau, TDP-43, and FUS, with FUS-positive ubiquitin inclusions being relatively rare.

questions.question_text: A 34-year-old woman presents with marked sudden decline in cognition and social withdrawal following a brief viral flu-like illness. This worsens over the following weeks with reduced level of consciousness, psychosis, repetitive chewing movements of her jaw and intermittent seizures. Which antibodies/antigens are implicated?
questions.explanation: The psychosis and repetitive chewing (oral dyskinesia) are most suggestive of NMDA receptor-mediated autoimmune encephalitis.

questions.question_text: What is the most common inclusion in Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD)?
questions.explanation: The classification of FTD is based on protein inclusions, which predominantly contain tau, TDP-43, or FUS. Tau-positive, amyloid-negative inclusions are the most common type in FTD.

questions.question_text: What is the pathophysiologic mechanism of Multisystem atrophy?
questions.explanation: Multisystem atrophy is classified as a synucleinopathy with distinctive inclusion bodies in glial cells containing alpha-synuclein, with no mutations in the alpha-synuclein gene found in MSA.

questions.question_text: Auto-immune encephalitis antibodies
questions.explanation: NMDA, DPPX, and IGCLON (LGI1) are all associated with different forms of autoimmune encephalitis. NMDA receptor antibodies are most common in NMDA receptor encephalitis, DPPX antibodies are found in DPPX-associated encephalitis, and IGCLON/LGI1 antibodies are associated with autoimmune limbic encephalitis.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which can be diagnosed during an episode of delirium?

options.text: A diagnosis of major depressive disorder

questions.explanation: The diagnosis for each of these illnesses cannot be made in the context of a delirium, as delirium may present with psychiatric symptoms that resolve when the underlying cause of the delirium resolves. Re FeRe NCe American Psychiatric Association. (2013). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed.). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.

His headaches occur at least twice a week without any specific precipitant. The pain is usually dull and bilateral, without ptosis, miosis, lacrimation, or conjunctival injection. What is the best treatment?

questions.question_text: A 14yearold male child comes to a pediatric neurologist for difficulty walking. His speech is dysarthric. Gait examination is notable for incoordination of lower limbs. Motor examination reveals weakness in the male child’s feet and legs, and sensory examination reveals decreased sensation in his feet. His feet also appear deformed, with fixed plantar flexion and high arch, and he has mild scoliosis. The neurologist suspects an inherited ataxia, and genetic testing is consistent with an autosomal recessive disorder related to triplet repeat expansions of the Frataxin gene. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of sturge– Weber syndrome

questions.explanation: Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive disorder related to triplet repeat expansions of the Frataxin gene. It is the most common inherited ataxia and affects most patients starting in early adolescence. Clinical presentation includes ataxic gait, dysarthria, limb weakness, sensory loss, peripheral neuropathy, scoliosis, and bilateral pes cavus (foot deformity). More than 75% of patients will live more than 34 years after disease onset.

questions.question_text: A previously healthy 84yearold male patient comes to the emergency room from his home via ambulance. On exam he is calm and cooperative but smells of urine. His wife reports that he has had nighttime incontinence and bouts of confusion, agitation, and visual hallucinations for 3 days. Which of the following should be the first step?

options.text: A diagnosis of order comprehensive metabolic panel

questions.explanation: This patient is displaying symptoms of delirium (impairment in awareness and attention, thought disorganization, agitation, and visual hallucinations). The first step is to first check a urinalysis to rule out an infection that could be causing his symptoms. Putting the patient in restraints or giving haloperidol is inappropriate at this time because he is calm and cooperative in the emergency department, and these should be considered only if less assertive behavioral measures such as redirection and deescalation fail. Starting donepezil is not appropriate because the patient is experiencing symptoms of delirium, not dementia. Filing for conservatorship is also unnecessary because the patient was seemingly healthy 3 days ago and is now experiencing a sudden change in his mental status.

questions.question_text: What is the most effective treatment for HIV encephalitis?
questions.explanation: Prompt administration of antiretroviral therapy is the most effective treatment for HIV encephalitis, addressing the underlying viral infection causing neurocognitive dysfunction.

questions.question_text: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder in patient on long-term ART shows

options.text: High CD8 count (does not normalize despite ART)

questions.explanation: Despite ART, CD8+ T-cell counts remain elevated and do not normalize. Additionally, brain atrophy, neuronal loss, and decreases in cortical gray matter are observed even in the first year of HIV infection and continue despite ART, reflecting ongoing CNS damage.

questions.question_text: Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) is increasingly used as a blood biomarker in neurological and psychiatric conditions. Elevated plasma GFAP most directly reflects:
questions.explanation: Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) is the major intermediate filament protein of astrocytes. When astrocytes are damaged, stressed, or undergo reactive astrogliosis, GFAP is released into the CSF and subsequently into blood. Plasma GFAP (measured using ultrasensitive SIMOA technology) is emerging as a biomarker in: Alzheimer's disease (elevated years before symptoms — reflects astrocytic response to amyloid pathology; may be superior to NfL for AD-specific prediction); traumatic brain injury (acute marker of severity); stroke; and increasingly in psychiatric research. In Alzheimer's disease, plasma GFAP outperforms NfL for distinguishing AD from other dementias and correlates with PET amyloid burden. Unlike NfL (which is non-specific for cell type), GFAP is relatively astrocyte-specific. Combining plasma GFAP + p-tau217 + NfL creates highly accurate blood-based dementia diagnostic panels (sensitivity/specificity >90%), potentially replacing invasive CSF analysis or expensive PET scans in future clinical practice.

questions.question_text: Which type of neuronal inclusions characterize Lewy body dementia?
questions.explanation: Lewy body dementia is characterized by alpha-synuclein accumulation in specific brain regions, forming Lewy bodies that are weakly eosinophilic, spherical, cytoplasmic inclusions.

questions.question_text: A 59yearold HIVpositive individual with documented cognitive decline exhibits left leg weakness. On examination, the individual has paresthesias bilaterally over his lower extremities, increased deep tendon reflexes, and spasticity. He also has urinary incontinence. Brain MRI shows moderate cortical and subcortical atrophy, but spinal cord MRI is unrevealing. Which of the following is the likely pathology in this individual’s spinal cord?

options.text: Vacuolar myelopathy of the lateral column

correct_answer.text: Vacuolar myelopathy of the lateral column

questions.explanation: The above case describes HIV myelopathy, which is characterized by a vacuolar myelopathy. This presents gradually, often with concurrent mild or major neurocognitive disorder due to HIV infection (itself newly added to the DSM5). Bilateral or unilateral sensory, motor, and autonomic involvement is present without a discrete sensory level. Lateral and posterior spinal columns are principally affected. MRI of the spinal cord is typically normal. In the above case, MRI of the brain shows cortical and subcortical atrophy, characteristic of neurocognitive disorders due to HIV infection. The case is not of transverse myelitis, which usually has bilateral presentation and a defined sensory level.

questions.question_text: A 40yearold female patient with migraines exhibits symptoms of unilateral throbbing pain, nausea, tinnitus, and ataxia. You suspect basilartype migraine. What is the recommended abortive treatment of headaches in this case?
questions.explanation: Basilar migraine is a rare type of migraine that presents with brainstemrelated aura symptoms without accompanying weakness. Aura is typically manifested by brainstem symptoms, including dysarthria, vertigo, diplopia, tinnitus, and ataxia. Whereas multiple disorders can resemble basilar migraine, the most important differential diagnoses include brainstem transient ischemic attack (TIA) or stroke. In the case of basilar migraine, triptans are contraindicated. Current recommendations suggest avoiding sympathomimetics such as triptans and ergotamine derivatives due to concerns for cerebral vasoconstriction. Ibuprofen can be used for abortive treatment. The other agents listed, verapamil and topiramate, are effective for basilar migraine prevention.

questions.question_text: Which treatment approach is most effective for HIV-related encephalitis?
questions.explanation: Prompt administration of antiretroviral therapy is the most effective treatment for HIV encephalitis, a complication affecting nearly half of HIV-infected patients. This addresses the underlying viral infection causing neuronal dysfunction.

questions.question_text: A man cannot properly use a hammer when given one, though he uses it correctly later. Which type of apraxia is this?
questions.explanation: Ideomotor apraxia is characterized by an inability to follow out learned tasks when given the necessary objects. The inability to use a hairbrush correctly (or hammer in this case) when handed the object, despite being able to perform the action later, is typical of ideomotor apraxia.

questions.question_text: At your next visit the individual continues to have moderate symptoms of depression. He explains, “I can’t tell if I’m coming or going. I keep forgetting things, and I’m clumsy.” He is concerned that he will “lose his mind” like his partner did. Despite his complaints of memory impairment, he is fully oriented, recalls three objects after 5 minutes, and has an intact fistedgepalm test. Urine toxicology screens have consistently been negative for any substances of abuse. Which of the following would be most appropriate at this time?

options.text: Evaluate for HIVassociated mild neurocognitive disorder.
Evaluate for HIV1- associated minor cognitive/ motor disorder.
Recommend lumbar puncture to rule out CNS infection.
Recommend brain MRI to evaluate for structural CNS disease.

questions.explanation: HIVassociated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) may occur in nearly half of patients with HIV disease, although 344 • PSyChIATRy thankfully in the era of combination antiretroviral therapy, HAND is now much more commonly either asymptomatic or mild rather than the devastating dementia prevalent through the early 1990s. The Frascati criteria published in 2007 represent the latest iteration of operationalized HAND diagnosis; these include HIVassociated asymptomatic neurocognitive impairment, mild neurocognitive disorder, and dementia. However, these cannot be diagnosed during clinical depression or within a month of active substance use. Management of depression takes precedence in this clinical situation. HIV1- associated minor cognitive/ motor disorder is an outdated term. Of note, whereas HAND is a more widely accepted diagnostic construct, DSM5 has adopted mild and major neurocognitive disorder due to HIV disease as new diagnostic categories.

questions.question_text: Liquid biopsies for CNS disorders involve analysis of circulating biomarkers in blood or CSF. Which technology has most enabled the detection of cell-free DNA (cfDNA) originating from brain cells in peripheral blood?
questions.explanation: Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) from dying cells (including neurons and glia) is released into the bloodstream, but the fraction originating from the brain is extremely small (<0.01% of circulating cfDNA). The breakthrough enabling brain-specific cfDNA detection is methylation-based tissue-of-origin analysis (liquid biopsy 'methylome profiling'). DNA methylation patterns are cell-type-specific and preserved on cfDNA fragments — allowing identification of the tissue of origin even at very low concentrations using methods like: bisulfite sequencing; methylation-sensitive restriction digestion; or targeted methylation arrays. Applications include: detecting neuron-derived cfDNA as a marker of neurodegeneration (elevated in Alzheimer's, ALS, TBI, ischaemic stroke); monitoring CNS tumour burden non-invasively (glioblastoma cfDNA); tracking treatment response. In psychiatry, the hypothesis is that elevated neuron-derived cfDNA may reflect neuronal death in neurodegenerative phases. This field is rapidly developing and complements protein biomarkers (NfL, GFAP, p-tau217) in the emerging 'multi-analyte' CNS liquid biopsy panel.

questions.question_text: The characteristic histopathological finding in Alzheimer's disease consisting of hyperphosphorylated tau protein arranged as neurofibrillary tangles is best described as:
questions.explanation: Neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) are composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein, a cytoskeletal element that appears basophilic and is a characteristic histopathological change in Alzheimer's disease.

questions.question_text: Confabulation is most commonly seen in which condition?
questions.explanation: Confabulation is commonly and characteristically seen in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, along with Alzheimer's disease in early stages, traumatic brain injury, and fetal alcohol spectrum disorder. It is the falsification of memory occurring in clear consciousness associated with organic pathology.

questions.question_text: Pick's bodies, pathognomonic for Pick's disease variant of frontotemporal dementia, are:

options.text: Intracytoplasmic tau and ubiquitin-reactive filamentous inclusions

correct_answer.text: Intracytoplasmic tau and ubiquitin-reactive filamentous inclusions

questions.explanation: Pick's bodies are argentophilic, tau and ubiquitin-reactive filamentous inclusions found within neurons, characteristic of Pick's disease variant of frontotemporal dementia.

questions.question_text: A 15yearold male with a history of diarrheal illness develops progressive bilateral weakness of the lower limbs over several days. Neurological exam is notable for areflexia. As the leg weakness worsens, the individual is unable to ambulate and is admitted to the hospital for monitoring of respiratory status. What bacterium is most commonly linked to this illness?
questions.explanation: This patient most likely has Guillain– Barré syndrome (GBS), which worldwide is the most common cause of acute flaccid paralysis. GBS is divided into the demyelinating form, acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy

questions.question_text: Which statement accurately describes Wernicke's aphasia?

options.text: Fluent, agrammatical speech with impaired comprehension
Loss of ability to speak and understand language

correct_answer.text: Fluent, agrammatical speech with impaired comprehension

questions.explanation: Wernicke's aphasia is characterized by fluent but often meaningless speech (wordy output) with significantly impaired comprehension of spoken language. The classic descriptor is Wernicke is wordy.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old male presents with a limbic encephalitis and impairment in short-term memory. He has started to develop seizures particularly affecting the face and arms, experiencing several episodes daily which has not responded well to anticonvulsants. He is found to have a low sodium upon completing investigations. Which antibodies/antigens are implicated?
questions.explanation: The faciobrachial seizures (brief, dystonic seizures affecting ipsilateral arm and face) and hyponatremia are most suggestive of LGI1-mediated autoimmune encephalitis.

questions.question_text: Which neurodegenerative disorder is linked to schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is most strongly linked to schizophrenia-like psychosis, occurring in 6-25% of patients with HD, particularly those with early onset. Schizophrenia-like psychosis also occurs in Friedreich's ataxia and has been identified at genetic and transcriptomic levels with ALS.

questions.question_text: Which autoimmune encephalitis antibody is most associated with optic nerve and spinal inflammation?
questions.explanation: Aquaporin-4 (AQP4) antibodies are associated with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, characterized by optic nerve and spinal cord inflammation.

questions.question_text: What is the most important pathophysiological finding in Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: The hallmark pathophysiology of Alzheimer's disease involves the deposition of extracellular beta-amyloid plaques and intracellular tau neurofibrillary tangles.

questions.question_text: A individual who is recovering from a stroke displays paucity of speech with excessive pauses or interruptions. He cannot repeat phrases. He can follow written commands. He appears quite frustrated with his situation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation here is consistent with Broca (by location) aphasia, which is also known as nonfluent or motor or expressive (by function) aphasia. The etiology is usually a middle cerebral artery stroke or another discrete structural lesion. The patient displays decreased production of words with pauses and cannot repeat phrases but has intact comprehension so that he or she can follow written ROPSYChIAtRIC DISORDERS • 111 commands. The patient is also aware of his or her problem, which causes frustration.

questions.question_text: In addition to documented infection with HIV and fulfillment of criteria for major or mild neurocognitive disorder (NCD), what other requirement must be met to qualify for a diagnosis of major or mild NCD due to HIV infection?

options.text: Presence of HIV in the cerebrospinal fluid.
Prominent early deficits in language production and comprehension.
Inability to attribute the NCD to non-HIV conditions (encompassing secondary brain diseases), another medical condition, or a mental disorder.
A diagnosis of presence of optic atrophy.

correct_answer.text: Inability to attribute the NCD to non-HIV conditions (encompassing secondary brain diseases), another medical condition, or a mental disorder.

questions.explanation: In addition to requiring fulfillment of criteria for major or mild NCD and documented infection with HIV, the diagnostic criteria for NCD due to HIV infection stipulate that the NCD is not better explained by non-HIV conditions, including secondary brain diseases such as progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy or cryptococcal meningitis; and that it is not attributable to another medical condition and is not better explained by a mental disorder. An NCD due to HIV infection generally shows a “subcortical pattern” with prominently impaired executive function, slowing of processing speed, problems with more demanding attentional tasks, and difficulty in learning new information, but fewer problems with recall of learned information. In major NCD, slowing may be prominent. Language difficulties, such as aphasia, are uncommon, although reductions in fluency may be observed. HIV pathogenic processes can affect any part of the brain; therefore, other patterns are possible. NCD due to HIV is more prevalent in individuals with high viral loads in the Neurocognitive Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE | 411 cerebrospinal fluid, but this is not a diagnostic criterion. Kayser-Fleisher rings are observed in Wilson’s disease, not HIV.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a core diagnostic criterion for Lewy body dementia?

options.text: Fluctuating cognition with notable variation in attention and alertness

correct_answer.text: Fluctuating cognition with notable variation in attention and alertness

questions.explanation: Fluctuating cognition with notable variation in attention and alertness is one of the two or more clinical features required for diagnosis of Lewy body dementia Evidence indicates-11.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the molecular basis of prion diseases?
questions.explanation: Prion diseases are characterized by abnormal protein misfolding, where the normal cellular prion protein (PrP^C) is converted to the pathogenic scrapie form (PrP^Sc), which accumulates and causes neurodegeneration.

questions.question_text: Which antibody is associated with autoimmune encephalitis?
questions.explanation: Multiple antibodies are associated with autoimmune encephalitis, including anti-NMDA receptor antibodies, anti-DPPX (dipeptidyl-peptidase-like protein-6), and anti-IGCLON (immunoglobulin superfamily containing leucine-rich repeat protein). These represent different forms of autoimmune encephalitis with varying clinical presentations.

questions.question_text: The classic clinical triad of Wernicke encephalopathy (WE) consists of mental status changes, ophthalmoplegia, and gait ataxia. This triad is present in what percentage of cases?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of WE is present in only 10% of cases. Conversely, other signs of disease such as hypothermia, vestibular dysfunction, and other ocular abnormalities can be present. Thus, reliance on the presence of the clinical triad as the sole criterion for disease is often inadequate and may lead to underdiagnosis.

questions.question_text: In HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder in patients on long-term antiretroviral therapy, which finding is observed?

options.text: Normalization of CD4 count to >500 cells/mm³
Elevated CD8+ T-cell counts that do not normalize despite ART

correct_answer.text: Elevated CD8+ T-cell counts that do not normalize despite ART

questions.explanation: CD8+ T-cell counts remain elevated during HIV infection and do not normalize despite long-term cART. While CD4+ counts may normalize with early treatment, elevated CD8+ counts persist, and neuronal loss and brain atrophy can continue even with ART.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which may prolong or worsen the individual’s condition?
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines are deliriogenic and should be avoided in delirium with the exception of alcohol withdrawal delirium or when used in combination with a neuroleptic for acute tranquilization. Anticholinergics should also be avoided because they worsen delirium. Antipsychotics such as quetiapine and risperidone are commonly used to manage the behavioral and psychological feature of delirium, though it bears noting that no medication is approved by the FDA for delirium. In a patient with Parkinson’s disease, quetiapine is typically preferred as a firstline agent. Buspirone does not have a role in acute management of delirium.

questions.question_text: Which gait pattern is characteristic of Huntington's disease?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is characterized by a lurching, chaotic gait.

questions.question_text: Memory affected in Korsakoff syndrome
questions.explanation: Episodic memory (recall of specific events) is characteristically impaired in Korsakoff syndrome. Implicit, semantic, and procedural memories are typically preserved, which is why patients can learn new skills despite not remembering the learning episodes.

questions.question_text: A 65yearold male patient reports gradualonset weakness of both thighs with unclear duration. He has had weakness of bilateral forearm for 3 years. There is no pain linked to weakness. Neurological examination is consistent with reduced bilateral knee reflexes, severe leg muscle weakness, and moderate weakness of thigh muscles. There is low muscle power of forearm flexors and extensors. Serum creatinine level is mildly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Inclusion body myositis is a T cell– mediated myotoxicity in which weakness in the lower extremity develops prior to in the upper extremity. The onset is insidious and sometimes illdefined by the patient. It is most common in men over 50 years of age. It typically involves quadriceps and forearm flexors and extensors. Polymyositis usually develops within weeks to months and involves proximal more than distal muscles. Dermatomyositis is a microangiopathy affecting skin and muscle. It presents with characteristic eyelid and extensor surface rash called heliotrope rash as well as the shawl sign. A quarter of patients with adultonset

questions.question_text: An 18yearold female has not reached menarche. Physical exam reveals normal female appearance, Tanner stage 5 breasts, and normal female external genitalia with labial masses. Chromosomal analysis reveals XY karyotype. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of androgen insensitivity syndrome

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of androgen insensitivity syndrome

questions.explanation: Androgen insensitivity syndrome was formerly called testicular feminization syndrome. Individuals with this syndrome have an XY karyotype, but the tissues are unable to use the testosterone or androgens. The patient appears as a normal female at birth. Sexual characteristics at puberty are usually those of a female. External genitalia appear female with possible labial masses suggestive of cryptorchid testes. 240 • PSYCHIATRY Patients typically present to a physician not having reached menarche well into adolescence. BIBLIoGRAPHY Sadock, B. J., Sadock, V. A., & Ruiz, P. (2014). Human sexuality and sexual dysfunction. In Kaplan and Sadock’s synopsis of psychiatry (11th ed., pp. 568– 569). questions.question_text: A 21yearold college senior comes to the student health center for 2 days of severe headache and fever. Physical exam reveals nuchal rigidity. The individual has no history of trauma or chronic infectious disease. His physician is concerned that he may have bacterial meningitis and performs blood work and lumbar puncture. Which of the following patterns of laboratory tests would be consistent with bacterial meningitis?

options.text: Total protein 250 mg/ dl, total WBC 1,000 cells/ µl, 90% neutrophils
Total protein 50 mg/dl, total WBC 150 cells/µl, 20% neutrophils
Total protein 85 mg/dl, total WBC 250 cells/µl, 25% neutrophils
Total protein 120 mg/dl, total WBC 400 cells/µl, 50% neutrophils
Total protein 300 mg/dl, total WBC 75 cells/µl, 15% neutrophils

correct_answer.text: Total protein 250 mg/ dl, total WBC 1,000 cells/ µl, 90% neutrophils

questions.explanation: Protein, total WBC, and neutrophils are elevated in bacterial meningitis. Choice B is consistent with aseptic meningitis. Choice C is consistent with tuberculous meningitis. Choice D is consistent with cryptococcal meningitis. Choice E is a distractor.

questions.question_text: Based on current evidence, thrombolysis for ischemic stroke reduces which of the following?

options.text: Risk of death rate and disability
Risk of nursing home placement only

questions.explanation: Treatment of strokes with thrombolysis improves chances of absence of disability but not survival.

questions.question_text: Disorders of consciousness include which of the following characteristics?
questions.explanation: Disorders of consciousness encompass global impairment of consciousness, disturbed sleep-wake cycles, and delirium characterized by disorganized thinking and cognitive dysfunction.

questions.question_text: Which histopathological finding in Alzheimer's disease consists of eosinophilic, rod-shaped cytoplasmic bodies?
questions.explanation: Hirano bodies are cytoplasmic, rod-shaped, and eosinophilic bodies found in Alzheimer's disease as part of its characteristic neuropathology.

questions.question_text: Prion disease has been reported to occur in patients of all ages, from the teenage years to late life. which of the following options best characterizes the time frame of disease progression?

options.text: A diagnosis of over one year.
A diagnosis of over several decades.

questions.explanation: Prion disease may develop at any age in adults—the peak age for sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is approximately 67 years, although it has been reported to occur in individuals spanning the teenage years to late life. Prodromal symptoms of prion disease may include fatigue, anxiety, problems with appetite or sleeping, or difficulties with concentration. After several weeks, these symptoms may be followed by incoordination, altered vision, or abnormal gait or other movements that may be myoclonic, choreoathetoid, or ballistic, along with a rapidly progressive dementia. The disease typically progresses very rapidly to the major level of impairment over several months. More rarely, it can progress over 2 years and appear similar in its course to other neurocognitive disorders.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old woman who recently underwent radiation treatment to her neck presented with ‘painful bones, renal stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans’. Which of the following condition is she most likely to be suffering from?
questions.explanation: This patient shows the classical features of hyperparathyroidism leading to hypercalcaemia, possibly precipitated by the irradiation to the neck. The psychic moans are most commonly due to depression and cognitive symptoms. These have been correlated with the degree of calcium elevation. In severe cases, confusion, catatonia, agitation, psychosis, and coma can occur. Most patients improve with treatment and correction of calcium levels. Hales RE and Yudofsky SC. The American Psychiatric Publishing Textbook of Neuropsychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences, 4th edn. American Psychiatric Press 2002, p. 867.

questions.question_text: Which condition is associated with LRRK2 mutation?
questions.explanation: LRRK2 mutation is seen in Parkinson's disease on chromosome 12p11.2. Other genes involved include PINK1, PARKIN, and SNCA.

questions.question_text: Which autoimmune encephalitis antibody is most associated with faciobrachial dystonic seizures and hyponatremia?
questions.explanation: LGI1-mediated autoimmune encephalitis presents with faciobrachial dystonic seizures (brief dystonic seizures affecting the face and arm), short-term memory impairment, and hyponatremia.

questions.question_text: Neurodegenerative disorder linked to Schizophrenia
questions.explanation: Both Huntington's disease and Friedreich's ataxia have documented associations with schizophrenia-like psychosis. Schizophrenia-like psychosis occurs in Huntington's disease in 6-25% of cases, and Friedreich's ataxia lists schizophrenia-like psychosis as one of its psychiatric manifestations.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a core clinical feature required for diagnosis of Lewy body dementia?

options.text: Memory loss as an early feature
Fluctuating cognition with notable variation in attention and alertness

correct_answer.text: Fluctuating cognition with notable variation in attention and alertness

questions.explanation: Fluctuating cognition with notable variation in attention and alertness is one of the core clinical features required (two or more features needed) for diagnosis of Lewy body dementia.

questions.question_text: What type of gait is characteristically seen in Huntington's disease?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is characterized by a lurching, chaotic gait, which reflects the involuntary movements and loss of motor control typical of this condition.

options.text: A diagnosis of frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder
Neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer’s disease
A diagnosis of major vascular neurocognitive disorder
Neurocognitive disorder due to traumatic brain injury

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of major vascular neurocognitive disorder

questions.question_text: What is the pathophysiologic mechanism of Korsakoff syndrome?

options.text: Damage to the medial prefrontal cortex
Loss of acetylcholine-producing neurons in the basal forebrain
Mammillary body and dorsomedial thalamus lesions due to thiamine deficiency
Loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra

correct_answer.text: Mammillary body and dorsomedial thalamus lesions due to thiamine deficiency

questions.explanation: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome results from thiamine deficiency, causing decreased functioning of enzymes in the tricarboxylic acid cycle. Mammillary body lesions are the classic autopsy sign, and diagnosis correlates best with dorsomedial thalamus lesions.

questions.question_text: In Lewy body dementia, alpha-synuclein accumulation occurs primarily in which of the following brain regions?

options.text: Temporal lobe, cingulate gyrus, frontal lobes, and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

correct_answer.text: Temporal lobe, cingulate gyrus, frontal lobes, and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

questions.explanation: Alpha-synuclein accumulation in Lewy body dementia occurs in the temporal lobe, cingulate gyrus, frontal lobes, and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus.

questions.question_text: There are various types of fronto-temporal dementia characterised by different pathological features. Which of the following is not a form of frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease typically affects the basal ganglia in the early phases of the disorder but then generally spreads to affect all cortical areas, and is caused by a different genetic mechanism (CAG repeat expansion) unrelated to frontotemporal dementia pathology. Progressive supranuclear palsy, while previously thought to be related to Parkinson's disease, is now recognized as related to frontotemporal dementia.

questions.question_text: Which variant of frontotemporal dementia is characterized by personality changes with preserved neurocognitive functioning in early stages?
questions.explanation: The behavioural variant of FTD is characterized by personality changes with neurocognitive functioning remaining relatively preserved in the early stages of the disease.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old lady with multiple sclerosis (MS) was presenting with a diagnosis of depression. She is on a number of medications for her MS. Of the following medication she is on, which is most likely to be linked to depressive symptoms?
questions.explanation: All of the present neuromedical treatments for MS including, corticosteroids, beta- interferons, glatiramer acetate, and immunosuppressants, are suspected to affect mood, at least in some individuals. Corticosteroids are associated with euphoria initially and long-term intake could lead to a depressive state. Initial studies of interferon beta-1b, an immunomodulatory cytokine used to reduce MS disease activity over prolonged periods, found increases in depression following initiation of treatment, and increased risk of suicide attempts. More recent studies have shown that this association may not be as robust as it was thought before. In fact, at least one study has shown that baseline depression levels actually drop following treatment with the medication. It is now thought that baseline or previous history of depression is more likely to predict the development of depressive symptoms during treatment. The BNF has a warning note asking clinicians to avoid the prescription of interferon beta in patients who have a history of severe depression and suicidal ideation. Depression is also a side-effect of Baclofen, but the association is less than with interferon beta. Feinstein A, O’Connor P and Feinstein K. Multiple Sclerosis, interferon beta-1b and depression. Journal of Neurology 2002; 249: 815–820. Goldman Consensus Group. The Goldman consensus statement on depression in multiple sclerosis. Multiple Sclerosis 2005; 11: 328–337.

questions.question_text: Pathological finding in Alzheimer's disease

options.text: Beta amyloid and Tau tangles (ubiquitin is a marker protein)
Only alpha synuclein and beta amyloid

correct_answer.text: Beta amyloid and Tau tangles (ubiquitin is a marker protein)

questions.explanation: The primary pathological hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease are beta-amyloid plaques and tau tangles. Ubiquitin is found as a component of these pathological structures, marking them for protein degradation.

questions.question_text: A man is unable to follow a sequence of actions in the correct order, such as taking a match out of a box and striking it. Which type of apraxia does he have?
questions.explanation: Ideational apraxia is characterized by an inability to follow a sequence of actions in the correct order. The example of taking a match out of a box and striking it demonstrates this specific deficit in sequential task execution.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is most commonly observed ocular finding present in Wernicke encephalopathy (WE)?
questions.explanation: Ophthalmoplegia is part of the classic WE triad. However, ophthalmoplegia remains only one of a variety of ocular findings that include nystagmus, sixth nerve palsy, ptosis, retinal hemorrhage, papilledema, and (less commonly) anisocoria or miosis. Complete ophthalmoplegia rarely occurs and likely represents progressive disease, and nystagmus (usually horizontal) is the most common ocular abnormality.

questions.question_text: What is the typical frequency of tremor in Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease is characterized by a resting tremor with a frequency of 4-6 Hz, typically around 5 Hz, which is slower than essential tremor.

questions.question_text: Wernicke's aphasia is characterized by:

options.text: Inability to repeat words despite preserved comprehension
Loss of speech with preserved understanding

questions.explanation: Wernicke's aphasia is characterized by fluent but meaningless speech with impaired receptive language (comprehension).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a type of fronto-temporal degeneration?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is not a type of fronto-temporal degeneration. FTD subtypes include behavioral variant FTD, primary progressive aphasia, semantic dementia, logopenic progressive aphasia, and progressive non-fluent aphasia.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is not a common neuropsychiatric feature seen in epilepsy?

options.text: A diagnosis of episodic mood disorder

questions.explanation: Ictal violence is extremely rare. Personality disorders are the most frequent neuropsychiatric presentation in epilepsy, with personality changes such as hyperor hyposexuality and religiosity. Interictal psychosis is more common than ictal psychosis and is schizophrenialike in presentation. Episodic mood disorders may involve depression or mania and are not as common as interictal psychosis. Re FeRe NCe Sadock, B. J., & Sadock, V. A. (2003). Kaplan and Sadock’s synopsis of psychiatry: Behavioral sciences/ clinical psychiatry (9th ed., pp. 358– 359). Philadelphia, PA: Lippincott Williams and Wilkins.

questions.question_text: A 75-year-old man has gradually changed in personality and behaviour over the last year with notably poor memory. His initial serological investigations are unremarkable. He has autonomic instability of heart rate and blood pressure and has experienced falls due to sudden 'jerks' in his legs associated with pain. His MRI shows mildly increased T2-FLAIR signaling in the medial temporal lobes. Which antibodies/antigens are implicated?
questions.explanation: The autonomic instability and 'jerks' (peripheral nerve hyperexcitability) are suggestive of CASPR2-mediated autoimmune encephalitis, with T2-FLAIR involvement of medial temporal lobes indicating limbic encephalitis.

questions.question_text: A man with bilateral coarse tremors and reduced eye gaze 5 years after a motor vehicle accident, whose tremors improve with sleeping tablets, most likely has
questions.explanation: While post-concussional syndrome typically presents within weeks to months of head injury, 5 years is beyond the typical window, making PTSD less likely; however, the chronic neurological features (tremor, gaze disturbance) with medication response suggest residual post-injury sequelae.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which bacterial causes of meningitis is a gramnegative diplococcus?
questions.explanation: Neisseria meningitidis is a gramnegative diplococcus.

questions.question_text: Which statement most accurately characterizes the diagnosis of neurocognitive disorder due to Huntington's disease (NCDHD)?

options.text: NCDHD is a disorder that requires positive neuroimaging for diagnosis.
NCDHD is a clinical diagnosis based on abnormal physical findings and family history/genetic findings.
NCDHD is a diagnosis that is best defined as patients who have a pillrolling tremor.
NCDHD requires neuroimaging as the primary diagnostic criterion.

correct_answer.text: NCDHD is a clinical diagnosis based on abnormal physical findings and family history/genetic findings.

questions.explanation: Genetic testing is the primary laboratory test for the determination of Huntington’s disease, which is an autosomal dominant disorder with complete penetrance. A diagnosis of definite Huntington’s disease is given in the presence of unequivocal extrapyramidal motor abnormalities in an individual with either a family history of Huntington’s disease or genetic testing showing a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene, located on chromosome 4.

questions.question_text: Which pathological finding is characteristic of Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: The hallmark pathological findings in Alzheimer's disease are beta-amyloid plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles. While ubiquitin is present in these structures, beta-amyloid is the primary pathological marker.

questions.question_text: A 38yearold female patient comes to the emergency room for altered mental status, including disorientation, confusion, and inability to register or recall new information. In the emergency room, she has a seizure. She is admitted to the hospital for workup. Laboratory testing is positive for antiNMDA receptor antibody. What should be included in the differential diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of creutzfeldt– Jakob disease

questions.explanation: In the past decade, paraneoplastic encephalitis has become better recognized. AntiNMDA receptor encephalitis is often, but not always, associated with tumors such as ovarian teratoma. The other options are not associated with the antiNMDA receptor antibody.
