Lancet Neurology, 2011 Jan; 10(1):63–74.

questions.question_text: How is Wilson's disease diagnosed once the central nervous system is affected?

options.text: By finding Kaiser-Fleischer rings in the cornea with a slit-lamp, though these are not universally present
By low ceruloplasmin and elevated copper in urine and liver biopsies
By MRI findings of lenticular nuclei involvement

correct_answer.text: By low ceruloplasmin and elevated copper in urine and liver biopsies

questions.explanation: A more reliable diagnosis depends on low ceruloplasmin and elevated copper in urine and liver biopsies, as Kaiser-Fleischer rings are not universally present.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which statements is accurate regarding frontotemporal dementia (FTD)?

options.text: Semantic dementia is the most commonly subtype
The frontal variant is distinguished by loss of word meaning and object recognition
40% of cases of FTD are familial autosomal dominant
Pick bodies contain tau and ubiquitin immunoreactivity
Pick’s disease is the most commonly histological variant

correct_answer.text: 40% of cases of FTD are familial autosomal dominant

questions.explanation: Forty per cent of cases of FTD are familial, mainly autosomal dominant. Mutations in the tau gene were fi rst found in FTD with parkinsonism linked to chromosome 17 (FTDP-17). Histologically FTD consist of fi ve types. The motor neuron type with inclusions reactive for ubiquitin but not for tau is the most frequent type. The second most common is a corticobasal degeneration type that is tau positive but with ubiquitin-negative inclusions. The third is Pick’s disease with neuronal loss, widespread gliosis, and infl ated neurons with inclusions positive for both tau and ubiquitin. The familial pattern has tau-positive inclusions in neurons and glial cells. Clinically frontal lobe variant accounts for the most common presentation (70%). They present with symptoms suggestive of frontal lobe dysfunction. Temporal variants are of two types: semantic and progressive aphasic. Semantic dementia accounts for about 15% of the presentation. They show progressive loss of word meaning and object or face identity. Ten per cent of cases are of the progressive aphasic type. Stein G and Wilkinson G. Seminars in General Adult Psychiatry, 2nd edn. RCPsych Publications, 2007, p. 519. Cummings JL and Mega MS. Neuropsychiatry and Behavioural Neuroscience, 2nd edn. Oxford University Press, 2003. p. 150.

questions.question_text: Which protein inclusion profile is most common in familial frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation: Familial FTD is characterized by tau-negative, ubiquitin-positive inclusions, often due to mutations in the progranulin (PGRN) gene. Pick's disease shows tau-positive, ubiquitin-positive inclusions. Overall, ubiquitin-positive, amyloid-negative inclusions are most common in FTD generally.

questions.question_text: A 12yearold female child has had difficulty walking since the age of 3 years. She also has gait abnormalities due to leg stiffness. Her symptoms are less prominent in the morning but worsen progressively as the day passes. She will most likely respond to which of the following medications?
questions.explanation: Doparesponsive dystonia (Segawa disease) usually presents in early childhood with symptoms of generalized dystonia and symptoms starting in one leg. Children with this condition are frequently misdiagnosed as having cerebral palsy. The key clinical feature is that the symptoms improve with sleep and worsen as the day progresses. Doparesponsive dystonia responds dramatically with a low dose of Ldopa. Other agents listed here have been studied for the treatment of various other types of dystonias. Botulinum toxin injection is beneficial with localized types of dystonia such as cervical dystonia and blepharospasm.

questions.question_text: What are the most important pathophysiological features of Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: The hallmark pathological features of Alzheimer's disease are extracellular beta-amyloid plaques and intracellular tau neurofibrillary tangles, both of which are essential to the disease process.

questions.question_text: In locked-in syndrome resulting from ventral pontine lesion, which of the following abilities is preserved?

options.text: Vertical eye movements and voluntary eye opening

correct_answer.text: Vertical eye movements and voluntary eye opening

questions.explanation: In locked-in syndrome from ventral pontine lesion, patients can open their eyes voluntarily and elevate and depress their eyes to command, while horizontal eye movements are usually lost and no other voluntary movement is possible.

questions.question_text: A 40yearold male patient with acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS) due to failed treatment with antiretroviral treatment exhibits acute central vision loss accompanied by floaters in his right eye. He denies eye pain but does have a headache. Ophthalmoscopy was suggestive of retinal atrophy in a “brushfire” pattern. What is the treatment?
questions.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) encephalitis and retinitis had a higher incidence in the era before antiretrovirals. CMV retinitis is still considered the most serious ocular complications of AIDS. When diagnosed, it is usually associated with either medication nonadherence or failed antiretroviral therapy. The presence of floaters is highly suggestive of CMV infection and is a good predictor of CMV retinitis. Clinical presentation and ophthalmoscopy are sufficient for diagnosis. Ganciclovir or its prodrug valganciclovir constitutes effective treatment for CMV encephalitis and retinitis.

questions.question_text: What is the most common finding in a newly diagnosed patient with Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation: Unilateral resting tremor is the most common presenting feature in Parkinson's disease. Adler and Ahlskog: Parkinson's disease and movement disorders Pg 72

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a true statement of Charles Bonnet Syndrome (CBS)?

options.text: CBS can last from a few days to years
A symptom of CBS is complex visual hallucinations
CBS can be caused by cataracts
CBS is a form of dementia
A symptom of CBS is visual hallucinations of simple repeated patterns

correct_answer.text: CBS is a form of dementia

questions.explanation: Charles Bonnet Syndrome (CBS) is not a mental illness, nor a form of dementia. It is caused by reducing vision in older age such as cataracts or macular degeneration. The person experiences visual hallucinations out of the blue that can either be simple vivid patterns or more complex visual hallucinations.

questions.question_text: Which class of drugs should be avoided in organic disinhibition?
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines should be avoided in organic disinhibition. There is some evidence that SSRIs and Trazadone may ameliorate disinhibition in fronto-temporal dementia

questions.question_text: George Smith, a 74-year-old retired teacher, presents to your outpatient clinic with his wife, Mary. She has expressed her concern that George has been spending an increasing amount of time in the betting office. His medical history includes; hypertension, Parkinson's disease, depression and gastrooesophageal reflux disease. Of the following medications he is taking, which is the most likely cause of pathological gambling?
questions.explanation: Impulsive and compulsive behaviour is a possible side effect of some medications used to treat Parkinson's disease, including levodopa. Although rare, it can have a profound effect on the patient and their family. It is important to discuss this risk with patients when prescribing medication for Parkinson's disease. (data from Parkinson's UK)

questions.question_text: The post-mortem examination done on an elderly gentleman who suffered from a slowly progressive non amnesic cognitive impairment, disinhibition and pill rolling tremors reveals ubiquitin inclusions. Which one among the following genes is most likely to reveal a mutation?
questions.explanation: This is a case of frontotemporal dementia (FTD). FTD is caused by mutations in progranulin (PGRN) especially in familial FTD. PGRN is located on chromosome 17q21.31.

questions.question_text: A mutation involving which of the following proteins is not associated with neurodegeneration?
questions.explanation: Huntingtin is associated with Huntington disease; Tau proteins with FTD; Synuclein with Lewy body dementia and Parkinson's; SOD mutation is associated with MND (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis). Tubulin mutations are accoiated with cancer syndromes mostly - recently an association has been demonstrated with pachygyria and lissencephaly - cortical folding disorders with no neurodegenerative features.

questions.question_text: Which of the following disorders is characterized by the presence of Hirano bodies and balloon cells (intracellular vacuoles)?
questions.explanation: Hirano bodies are bright eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions which occur in a wide variety of conditions, especially amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and Parkinsonism-dementia complex, Alzheimer's disease, Pick's disease and 'normal' elderly individuals. In Pick's disease (a form of fronto-temporal dementia), there are two distinctive histologic features: swelling of neurons (resulting in ballooned Pick cells) and an inclusion within the perikaryon, most often in layer II (resulting in a Pick body). Pick bodies are usually found in limbic, paralimbic, and ventral temporal lobe cortex. Both Hirano bodies and balloon cells are seen in fronto-temporal dementia

questions.question_text: ECG changes in Huntington's disease include an increase in the incidence of
questions.explanation: There is increasing evidence that, in Huntington's, in addition to central nervous system pathology, peripheral tissues may also be affected. In particular, animal models of HD show significant cardiac dysregulation. Patients with HD show sympathovagal disturbance and increased rates of sudden cardiac death. Nearly 25% of HD patients show an abnormal ECG. Bradycardia, prolonged intraventricular conduction and unexplained QTc elevation were the most commonly observed changes. Ref: http://www.neurology.org/content/84/14_Supplement/P5.294

questions.question_text: A 77-year-old Vietnam War veteran presents with shooting pain in his back. On neurological examination, you find light near dissociation of Argyll Robertson Pupil. Which of the following is true?

options.text: Consensual light reflex will be present
Both light and accommodation reflex will be present
Afferent pupillary defect will be seen

questions.explanation: ARP - Argyll Robertson Pupil (note: Accommodation Reflex Present -light reflex absent) is due to an afferent defect in the pupillary reflex pathway - most probably a pretectal lesion.

questions.question_text: Mrs. X is an 83-year-old lady who has been diagnosed with early stages of Alzheimer's disease. The brain region, which could show prominent changes, is;
questions.explanation: Profound loss of layer two entorhinal cortex neurons occurs in very mild Alzheimer's disease. The entorhinal cortex plays a crucial role connecting the neocortex and hippocampal formation and is affected severely likely contributing to memory impairment.

questions.question_text: A 33-year-old man presents with anxiety and depression. Soon he develops rapidly progressive cognitive impairment with myoclonus, ataxia and eventually akinetic mutism. Characteristic pathological change expected in brain autopsy, in this case, is
questions.explanation: The description suggests CJD. Microscopically CJD shows a spongiform encephalopathy secondary to neuropil vacuolisation.

questions.question_text: The pathological factor that correlates most with cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease is
questions.explanation: A staging scheme devised by Braak and Braak (1995) is widely used to describe the extent of tangle related abnormalities (distribution from entorhinal cortex to isocortex) in AD and correlates well with the severity of dementia. Stages V-VI operationally define AD.

questions.question_text: Knife blade atrophy is seen in
questions.explanation: Knife-blade type atrophy refers to the marked atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes with relative sparing of parietal and occipital lobes in patients with Pick's disease.

questions.question_text: Alpha-synuclein is a major constituent of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Lewy bodies are weakly eosinophilic, spherical, cytoplasmic inclusions. Lewy bodies in Parkinson's disease and DLB contain accumulations of alpha-synuclein

questions.question_text: The macroscopic changes seen in Alzheimer's disease includes
questions.explanation: The macroscopic changes in Alzheimers disease would include Enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles, global brain atrophy, reduction in brain weight and sulcal widening. Neuronal loss, senile plaques, neurofibrillary tangles, reactive astrocytosis and shrinking of dendritic branching are the microscopic changes seen in the cerebral cortex in Alzheimers disease. Cerebral atrophy and ventricular enlargement are macroscopic changes.

questions.question_text: Depigmentation of the substantia nigra is seen in which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation: The macroscopic changes in idiopathic Parkinsons disease would include depigmentation of the substantia nigra, particularly the zona compacta, and depigmentation of the locus coereleus and diffuse cortical atrophy. The histological changes in idiopathic Parkinsons disease would include Reactive astrocytosis, neuronal loss, Presence of Lewy bodies in different areas such as the substantia nigra, locus cereleus, dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, hypothalamus, nucleus basalis of meynert, Edinger-Westphal nucleus and raphe nuclei.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the difference between CJD and vCJD? The variant CJD has

options.text: Absence of florid plaques on autopsy

questions.explanation: In 1996, a new type of CJD called vCJD (variant CJD) was reported. Variant CJD appears to affect younger people than the other forms of the disease, with an average age of death of 29 years. Death occurs on an average within 14 months.

questions.question_text: Marked atrophy of the caudate nucleus is seen in which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation: Macroscopic findings in Huntington's disease include 1. Small brain with reduced mass 2. Marked atrophy of the corpus striatum, particularly the caudate nucleus 3. Marked atrophy of the cerebral cortex, particularly the frontal lobe gyri 4. Dilatation of the lateral and third ventricles. Histological changes in Huntington's disease would include neuronal loss in the cerebral cortex and neuronal loss in the corpus striatum and astrocytosis in the affected regions.

questions.question_text: Arteriosclerotic changes in major arteries are most commonly found in which of the following types of dementia?
questions.explanation: In multi-infarct dementia, brain damage due to multiple cerebral infarcts leads to local or general brain atrophy and ventricular enlargement. The presence of arteriosclerotic changes is commonly noted.

questions.question_text: In those with Mild Cognitive Impairment, which of the following biomarkers can detect worsening cognitive function?
questions.explanation: Individuals with early Alzheimer's dementia have reduced CSF beta-amyloid and increased levels of CSF tau and phosphorylated tau. The CSF tau/amyloid beta ratio is nearly 5 times higher in those who later convert to full-blown Alzheimer's dementia compared to non-converters. Increased CSF tau/A-beta (amyloid) ratios show strong promise as a preclinical biomarker to predict future dementia in cognitively normal older adults. Fagan et al., Arch Neurol. 2007 Mar;64(3):343-9.

questions.question_text: The spongiform appearance of brain tissue in CJD is due to
questions.explanation: Microscopically CJD shows a spongiform encephalopathy secondary to neuropil vacuolisation.

questions.question_text: Lewy bodies are eosinophilic, haloed, intra neuronal inclusions. They contain which of the following materials?
questions.explanation: Lewy bodies contain Tau protein, Ubiquitin, protein neurofilaments, granular material, dense core vesicles and microtubule assembly protein. In Lewy body dementia, the density of Lewy bodies is much higher in the cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus and temporal cortex.

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old lady is a known alcoholic. She drinks in binges and presents with deficits in new learning though she could retain messages long enough to hold a conversation. The most prominent pathology in this patient will be seen in
questions.explanation: Wernicke's encephalopathy is characterized by degenerative changes including gliosis and small hemorrhages in structures surrounding the third ventricle and aqueduct (i.e. the mamillary bodies, hypothalamus, mediodorsal thalamic nucleus, colliculi, and midbrain tegmentum), as well as cerebellar atrophy.

questions.question_text: The immunological staining used in detection of Pick's disease is
questions.explanation: A variety of stains can be used to visualise Pick bodies and Pick cells, but the most efficient and highly specific method is to use immunohistochemical staining with anti-tau and anti-ubiquitin antibodies. The neurofibrillary tangles of Alzheimer's can be stained with antibodies to basic fibroblast growth factor, amyloid P, and heparan sulfate glycosaminoglycan.

questions.question_text: The neuropathological findings in Punch Drunk syndrome include which of the following changes?
questions.explanation: Dementia pugilistica (DP) is a type of neurodegenerative disease that can affect around 15% of boxers who suffer concussions after 12-16 years of boxing on average. Symptoms and signs of DP develop progressively over a long latent period.Histological changes in Punch Drunk syndrome (Dementia Pugilistica) would include neuronal loss and neurofibrillary tangles. Thinning of the corpus callosum, perforation of the septum pellucidum and ventricular enlargement is also seen in this condition.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a protective factor against Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: Apolipoprotein e2 allele is a proven protective factor against Alzheimer's disease. Other possible protective factors are smoking, NSAIDs, oestrogen, premorbid intelligence and education.

questions.question_text: Hirano bodies are seen in brain autopsy of a patient who had a history of cognitive impairment. Which of the following diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Hirano bodies are rod-shaped eosinophilic bodies in the cytoplasm of neurons that may be set free in the extracellular space if the neuron dies. Hirano bodies seen in Alzheimer's are intracellular aggregates of actin and actin-associated proteins. They are frequently seen in hippocampal pyramidal cells

questions.question_text: Autopsy of an elderly man who suffered from marked tremors and a progressive cognitive decline shows cells negative for tau protein. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lewy bodies that are seen in diffuse Lewy body disease (dementia), rarely have any tau protein deposits. They are primarily made of alpha synuclein and ubiquitin which are tau negative.

questions.question_text: Which of the following has no evidence-based support when prescribing antidementia drug donepezil? It

options.text: Improves the amount of daily activities in some patients
Reduces the progression of cognitive decline

questions.explanation: There is strong evidence that donepezil has efficacy against the three major domains of Alzheimer's disease symptoms, namely functional ability, behavior, and cognition. The strongest evidence is for improvement or less deterioration in global outcomes and cognition in the short to medium term. There is limited evidence that improved global outcomes are maintained in the long term and clear evidence to support long-term maintenance of cognitive benefits. Also, donepezil appears to maintain function in the long term, and there is some level 1 and two evidence of improved or limited deterioration in behavior or mood in the short to medium term. Despite donepezil's effects on major symptoms of Alzheimer's disease, its impact on patients' quality of life has not been consistently demonstrated, perhaps reflecting the difficulty of assessing this aspect in this patient population. Donepezil may also lessen caregiver burden. There is limited and conflicting weak evidence that long-term donepezil treatment delays time to institutionalization. Birks JS, Harvey R. Donepezil for dementia due to Alzheimer's disease. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2003;(3): CD001190.
